title: C-Style Arrays and C-Strings
summary: `int arr[5]{};` is the raw array inherited from C. Passed to a function it **decays** to a pointer and loses its length. A C-string is a `char` array ending in `'\0'`. Learn them to read existing code; write `std::array`, `std::vector` and `std::string`.
markdown:
## Why learn the old way? C++ grew out of C and still contains C's arrays and strings. New code should not use them, but operating-system interfaces, C libraries and thirty years of existing code do. You need to read them fluently. ## C-style arrays ```cpp #include #include int main() { int scores[5]{ 90, 80, 70, 60, 50 }; scores[0] = 100; std::cout << std::size(scores) << '\n'; // 5 return 0; } ``` ``` scores ┌─────┬─────┬─────┬─────┬─────┐ │ 100 │ 80 │ 70 │ 60 │ 50 │ └─────┴─────┴─────┴─────┴─────┘ address: 0x100 0x104 0x108 0x10C 0x110 each int is 4 bytes ``` The length goes in square brackets after the name. There is no `.size()`, no `.at()` and no bounds checking of any kind. ## Array decay This is the property that makes C-style arrays hazardous. ```cpp void print(int arr[]) // this really means: int* arr { std::cout << sizeof(arr) << '\n'; // 8: the size of a pointer } ``` ```mermaid flowchart LR A["int scores[5]
knows it has 5 elements"] -->|"passed to a function"| P["int*
only an address:
the length is gone"] ``` When a C-style array is passed to a function, it converts to a pointer to its first element. This is **decay**. The function receives an address and nothing else, so the length has to travel as a separate argument: ```cpp void print(const int* values, std::size_t length); ``` Nothing ensures the two stay in agreement. A wrong length means reading or writing beyond the array: the classic **buffer overflow**. ## Pointer arithmetic Because an array name converts to a pointer, pointers can be used to walk an array. | Expression | Meaning | |---|---| | `int* p{ scores };` | `p` points at `scores[0]` | | `*(p + 2)` | The element two places on: `scores[2]` | | `p[2]` | Exactly the same thing | | `++p;` | `p` now points at the next element | ``` p p+1 p+2 p+3 p+4 ▼ ▼ ▼ ▼ ▼ [100] [80] [70] [60] [50] ``` Adding 1 to a pointer moves it by one **element**, not one byte. For an `int*` that is 4 bytes. In fact `a[i]` is defined as `*(a + i)`. ## C-strings A C-string is an array of `char` with a **null terminator**, the character `'\0'` (value 0), marking the end. ```cpp char name[]{ "Ada" }; // four chars: 'A' 'd' 'a' '\0' ``` ``` ┌───┬───┬───┬────┐ │ A │ d │ a │ \0 │ └───┴───┴───┴────┘ ``` No length is stored. Every function that needs it walks the characters until it meets the terminator. | Fact | Consequence | |---|---| | A literal `"hello"` is a `const char[6]` | Five letters plus the terminator | | Functions live in `` | `std::strlen`, `std::strcpy`, `std::strcmp` | | None of them check sizes | Copying into too small an array overflows it | | `==` on two `char*` compares **addresses** | Not the text | Converting between the two worlds is easy: ```cpp const char* greeting{ "Hello" }; std::string s{ greeting }; // C-string to std::string const char* raw{ s.c_str() }; // std::string to C-string, for a C function ``` ## The modern equivalents | C style | Modern C++ | |---|---| | `int a[5];` | `std::array` | | An array whose size is decided while running | `std::vector` | | `char s[100];` or `const char*` | `std::string` or `std::string_view` | | `std::strlen(s)` | `s.length()` | | `std::strcmp(a, b) == 0` | `a == b` | | A pointer and a length | `std::span` | ### `std::span` `std::span` (C++20) is to arrays what `std::string_view` is to text: a pointer and a length carried together, with no ownership. ```cpp #include #include #include int sum(std::span data) { int total{ 0 }; for (int x : data) { total += x; } return total; } int main() { int raw[]{ 1, 2, 3 }; std::vector v{ 4, 5 }; std::cout << sum(raw) << ' ' << sum(v) << '\n'; // 6 9 return 0; } ``` One function accepts a C-style array, a `std::array` or a vector, and the length can never disagree with the data. ## Where you will still meet them | Place | Example | |---|---| | The program's command line | `int main(int argc, char* argv[])`: see [[5.10 Function Pointers, Callbacks and Command-Line Arguments]] | | C libraries and operating-system functions | They take `const char*` and pointer-plus-length pairs | | Older code and tutorials | Anything written before about 2011 | ## Check yourself ```quiz ? What is array decay? - An array slowly losing its values as the program runs + A C-style array turning into a pointer, losing its length - An array being destroyed at the end of its scope - A `std::array` converting to a `std::vector` > Passed to a function, a C-style array becomes a pointer to element 0, so the function no longer knows how many elements there are. ? How many bytes does the literal `"cat"` occupy? - Three + Four - Eight - It depends on the computer > Three letters plus the `'\0'` terminator that marks the end of a C-string. ? If `p` is an `int*`, how far does `p + 1` move? - One byte, whatever the type - Four elements, one for each byte - It does not compile + One element: `sizeof(int)` bytes > Pointer arithmetic counts in elements of the pointed-to type, so `p + 1` is the next `int`. ? What does `std::span` carry? + A pointer to the first element and a count, owning nothing - A full copy of the elements - Only a pointer, like array decay - The elements and their capacity, like a vector > A `std::span` is a view: pointer plus length. It does not own the data, so the data must outlive it. ```
ideas:
1. Print `sizeof` of a C-style array in `main`, and again inside a function it is passed to. Explain the difference.
2. Walk a C-string with a pointer until you reach `'\0'` to compute its length yourself.
3. Rewrite a function that takes `(const int* values, std::size_t length)` to take a `std::span<const int>`.
